_readme: Cross-language corpus for hardening dynamic URL path segments.
Two clients build URLs for one API. If they disagree about what a hostile
user_id/app_name/filename becomes, one of them is reachable off-route while
the other is not — and neither client's own tests can see that. This file is
the single source of truth both read:
Python     tests/unit/test_v2_path_encoding.py
TypeScript ../../packages/sdk/test/parity.test.ts
Two lists, because the clients are deliberately no longer identical:
`cases`   values BOTH clients accept. Each names the path the request must
end up on; both clients must build it byte-for-byte, so a change
to either encoder goes red. `typescript_path` + `why_divergent`
mark a place they legitimately differ, and a divergence is only
allowed to be cosmetic — enforced ROUTE-aware, not decode-aware:
the RAW `/` count must match, because the number of components is
what selects the route. (Comparing only the decoded strings would
accept `/users/a%2Fb` against `/users/a/b`, which is two different
endpoints and is the whole bug.) There is no opt-out from that rule:
the three routes that declare `{filename:path}` all sanitize the value
to a basename in the handler, so a divergence there would not be free
either.
`refused` values the Python client refuses outright (m8tes.ValidationError).
Encoding them is not enough: an ASGI server percent-decodes the path
before routing it, so an escaped separator still selects a different
route, and the empty string and the dot segments resolve onto the
collection or the parent. `typescript_path` records the URL the
TypeScript client builds for the same input TODAY. That is a pin,
not an endorsement: the two clients are not yet aligned here, and
recording the current value is what makes any change to it
deliberate and visible. When both refuse, the field goes away and
both halves assert a throw.
`$VALUE` is substituted with the case's `value` before the call is made.

cases.name: an already-encoded slash is encoded again, never passed through
a question mark would turn the rest of the value into query params
a hash would truncate the path at the fragment
a colon must not read as a scheme or a port
dots that are not a whole dot segment stay literal and harmless
spaces and non-ASCII round-trip as UTF-8 percent escapes
a newline is escaped rather than carried into the request line
unreserved characters are left alone by both
sub-delims RFC 3986 reserves but encodeURIComponent leaves literal
cases.why_divergent: encodeURIComponent exempts !*'() from its escape set; Python's quote(safe="") follows RFC 3986 and escapes them. Both decode to the same segment server-side and neither can leave it, so this is cosmetic — asserted as such by both halves rather than waved through.

cases.name: an app slug with metacharacters stays one segment
a backslash is encoded, not refused and not translated to a separator
a run filename is one segment, encoded like any other

refused.name: a slash reaches a sibling sub-route once the server decodes
refused.note: An escaped separator still selects a different route once decoded.

refused.name: climbing out of the resource prefix entirely
refused.note: The original report: this left the resource prefix entirely.

refused.name: an empty segment collapses onto the collection route
refused.note: An empty segment resolves onto the collection route.

refused.name: a lone dot collapses onto the collection route
refused.note: requests resolves the dot segment in prepare_url.

refused.name: a lone dot-dot climbs to the parent
refused.note: requests resolves this to the parent before the request leaves the process; escaping does not survive requote_uri either.

refused.name: a trailing separator produces a 307 the client follows to a raw dot segment
refused.note: Starlette's redirect_slashes answers 307 and requests follows the Location verbatim without re-preparing the URL, so a raw `..` reaches the wire. It lands on the {user_id} route with user_id='..' rather than climbing — but the SDK should not be emitting a dot segment at all.

refused.name: an app slug carrying a separator
refused.note: Same class as the users case, on the other string-typed segment.

refused.name: a run filename carrying a separator, which the handler rejects anyway
refused.note: The route declares {filename:path}, but its handler sanitizes the filename to a basename, so a value carrying a separator cannot resolve there either — the SDK refuses it with the same rule as every other segment.
